# Data Analytics {#sec-analytics}

This section covers all analytical methods applied to the prepared data:
descriptive spatial analytics, predictive modelling of demand (SVM and
neural networks), and reinforcement learning for smart charging.

## Predictive Analytics (SVM & Neural Networks) {#sec-prediction}

<!-- ASSIGNMENT Task 3 — Predictive Analytics (a) SVM and (b) Neural Networks:

  Sunday 10-11am on the outskirts?".

Fleet planning needs to know where and when demand will appear before the shift
starts, so we predict trip starts per spatial unit and time bucket from calendar,
location, weather, and POI features alone, without extrapolating one hour from
the previous one. The question the model answers is a scenario question: how much
demand to expect on a rainy Sunday morning on the outskirts. We compare two model
families on this task, a Support Vector Machine (fitted both directly on demand
and on the residual over a historical-mean baseline) and a feedforward neural
network, across six grids that cross three spatial units (H3 resolution 7, census
tract, community area) with hourly and daily time bins. Both are scored against
the same historical-mean baseline, which is what lets us ask whether a learned
model, and a deep one in particular, is worth its added complexity here.

### Problem Setup and Validation Strategy

<!-- Sources: docs/report_content_guide.md 4.2 "Data setup"; notebooks
3.1 FeatureEngineering.ipynb, 3.2 Prediction_CommonGround.ipynb.
Feature engineering itself is described in @sec-data-prep. -->

The prediction target is `Total_Trip_Start`, the number of trips beginning in a
given spatial unit during a given time bucket. Prediction is scenario-conditioned
rather than autoregressive: no model sees the previous bucket's demand, only the
cell's identity and location, the calendar, the weather, and the POI counts for
that cell. That restriction comes from the assignment brief, and it also matches
the client's actual planning problem, which is positioning vehicles ahead of a
shift rather than reacting to the hour just past. What each model *fits* is not
identical to the target itself, since the residual SVM predicts a correction to a
baseline rather than demand directly; the two strategies are described in the
subsections below.

Every model is trained on six grids: three spatial units (H3 resolution 7 with
108 active hexagons, 496 active census tracts, and 77 community areas) crossed
with hourly and daily bins. Resolution 8 is explored descriptively in @sec-eda
but excluded from modelling [GAP: state why res 8 was dropped before modelling;
the pipeline filters it out without recording a reason], and inactive units,
those with no pickups anywhere in the observation window, are dropped during grid
construction (@sec-data-prep). Sparsity differs sharply across the six: the share
of zero-demand rows runs from 0.8% at community/daily to 96.5% at census/hourly.
That spread drives the sampling decisions taken separately for each model family
below.

The reference point throughout is a historical mean per spatial unit, keyed by
month and day of week on the daily grids and additionally by hour on the hourly
ones. It is computed on the training split alone and merged into validation and
test, so it carries no future information, and it serves twice over: as the
`base_demand` feature available to both models and as the benchmark for the skill
score, `1 - MAE_model / MAE_baseline`. Skill rather than raw MAE is reported
because mean demand differs by roughly a factor of 80 across the six grids, which
makes absolute errors incomparable between them. Both model families fit in
`log1p` space and invert with `expm1`, clipped at zero, so every metric quoted
here is in count space.

Train, validation and test are cut along the calendar rather than drawn at
random. The earliest 50% of unique dates train the models, the next 20% serve for
validation, and the final 30% are held back for testing [GAP: state the actual
date boundaries of the three splits]. A random row-level split would place adjacent
hours of the same cell on both sides of the boundary and leak autocorrelated
demand into the test set, and it would also contaminate `base_demand`, which is
estimated from training dates only. Model selection, covering feature sets,
kernels, architectures, and hyperparameters, is therefore carried out on the
validation split, with the test split scored once for the selected models.
[GAP: this single-scoring discipline holds for the SVM notebooks; confirm and
state plainly how the NN's per-level scores were obtained before finalising, see
@sec-nn.] [GAP: one EDA notebook argues the final week of collection is
incomplete and should be excluded; no such truncation exists in the pipeline.
Resolve and state here, or move to the limitations.]

### Support Vector Machine

<!-- Source notebooks: notebooks/3.2 PredictionCommonGround.ipynb (shared
registry, sampling, scoring), 3.2a PredictionSVMStandard.ipynb (direct),
3.2b PredictionSVMResidual.ipynb (residual). Validation figures below are read
from the post-zero-mile-drop artifacts in models_predictions/SVR/. -->

Two SVR strategies are trained on identical splits, samples and candidate feature
sets, differing only in what they are asked to predict. The direct model
regresses `log1p(Total_Trip_Start)` on the feature block and converts predictions
back with `expm1`, clipped at zero. The residual model predicts the log-space
correction to the historical mean instead, `log1p(demand) - log1p(base_demand)`,
and reconstructs counts as `expm1(log1p(base_demand) + correction_hat)`; it never
sees the raw target, only how far a given cell and time bucket departs from its
own history. The motivation is that `base_demand` already carries much of the
predictable signal, so a model asked to reproduce it from scratch spends its
capacity on something the pipeline has already computed, whereas the correction
is the part that genuinely has to be learned. Since that correction has a far
smaller scale and variance than `log1p(demand)`, hyperparameters tuned for one
target do not transfer to the other, and the residual model is therefore tuned
from scratch rather than inheriting the direct model's settings.

Both strategies are bounded by fitting cost. SVR is O(n²) to fit, which puts
training splits of up to 6.2 million rows out of reach, so each level is fitted
on a class-balanced sample: 4,000 rows per class for the kernel scan and 8,000
per class for the grid search, with selection scored on a 50,000-row validation
subsample and only the level's winner re-scored on the full validation split.
Balancing rather than uniform sampling is what makes such a small sample usable,
since at h3_7/hourly roughly 94% of rows are zero and a uniform draw would be
almost entirely empty cells; where a level is not zero-inflated the zero class
runs out and the sample tilts non-zero on its own. Validation and test are always
evaluated at natural prevalence, so training and evaluation deliberately see
different class mixes.

Tuning then proceeds in two stages per level and feature set. A kernel scan
compares linear, polynomial and RBF at fixed `C=1` and `gamma="scale"`, judged by
validation R² in count space, and the winning kernel goes into a three-fold grid
search over `C` in {1, 10, 50} and `gamma` in {scale, 0.05, 0.2}, extended by
`degree` in {2, 3} where the polynomial kernel wins, scored by count-space MAE.
Four feature sets compete at every level (a basic calendar, location and history
block, then that block plus weather, plus POI, and plus both), with the winner
taken on validation R² in count space. The direct notebook runs this through
sklearn's `GridSearchCV`; the residual notebook reimplements the identical grid
as a manual K-fold loop, because a standard scorer never sees a row's
`base_demand` and so cannot turn a predicted correction back into a trip count.
LIBSVM's iteration count is capped, as some `C`/`gamma` combinations otherwise
run without converging.

#### Validation Results

{{< embed "notebooks/3.2b PredictionSVMResidual.ipynb#tbl-svr-direct-vs-residual-final" >}}

{{< embed "notebooks/3.2b PredictionSVMResidual.ipynb#fig-svr-direct-vs-residual-final" >}}

The direct model does not beat the historical mean it was given as a feature. At
five of six levels its tuned winner is worse than the baseline on validation MAE,
from -3.5% at community/daily down to -35.5% at census/hourly, and the single
level it wins, h3_7/daily, it wins by 0.2%, which is a tie in all but sign.
Predicting the correction instead improves the skill score at all six levels, but
the improvement is uneven and mostly modest: community/daily is the one clear
win at +5.3% (R² = 0.970), h3_7/daily turns its tie into a slim +1.2%, h3_7/hourly
(+0.3%) and census/daily (+0.3%) remain ties, and community/hourly stays just
short of the baseline at -1.0%.

The exception is census/hourly, the sparsest grid at 96.5% zero rows, which loses
heavily under both strategies (-35.5% direct, -32.1% residual). Its error profile
is diagnostic: MAE skill is deeply negative while RMSE skill is roughly flat
(+0.7% residual). A model trained on a balanced sample and scored at natural
prevalence predicts a little too much demand across a very large mass of empty
cells, which accumulates in MAE but barely registers in an RMSE dominated by the
few large errors at busy cells.

Two patterns hold across the grid. Daily aggregation beats hourly at all three
spatial resolutions under both strategies, consistent with hourly bins being
sparser and noisier. And kernel selection splits cleanly between the strategies:
every direct winner is RBF, while four of six residual winners are linear (both
h3_7 levels, census/hourly and community/daily). This is a property of the
transform rather than a preference for simplicity. A linear model in log space is
unbounded, and `expm1` turns a moderately wrong log prediction into an enormous
count, so the direct target needs a bounded nonlinear fit; the residual's small
scale never pushes the reconstruction into that regime. All six residual winners
also settled at `C=1`, against direct winners spread from `C=1` to `C=50`.
[GAP: `C=1` is the lowest value in the search grid, so these winners sit on a
grid edge. Either extend the grid downwards or confirm that validation
performance is flat there before reporting the setting as converged.]

The test split is untouched at this stage. It is scored once, for the selected
models, in the comparison against the neural network.

#### Shortfalls and Improvement Levers {#sec-svm-shortfalls}

<!-- Sources: docs/report_content_guide.md 4.2 "Shortfalls & improvement levers";
permutation/ablation figures from 3.2a (in-memory, see fig-svr-feature-importance).
The two-stage-search check below was re-verified against the artifacts on disk;
see the paragraph on residual_kernelgrid for what that verification found. -->

The plainest shortfall is how little either strategy gains on the historical mean.
That is less a tuning failure than a consequence of the framing: with
autoregressive signal ruled out, cell identity plus calendar sits close to the
ceiling of what is predictable here, and a historical mean over those same keys is
already close to optimal. It also bounds what the obvious remedy would buy. Each
level is fitted on at most 16,000 rows because SVR's quadratic fitting cost makes
anything larger impractical, but more rows of the same features are unlikely to
clear a ceiling set by the features themselves. The lever worth testing is how the
sample is drawn rather than how much of it is used, and natural-prevalence
training is the untested alternative that two separate results point towards: the
census/hourly collapse described above, and the zero-demand behaviour below.

That second result is a specific and fixable failure mode. On the held-out
comparison the residual model is worse than the baseline precisely on cells whose
actual demand turns out to be zero, where the neural network is better; the
correction term does not shrink to zero where it should. Because zero rows are
between 79% and 94% of all rows depending on the level, that one segment carries
disproportionate weight in any aggregate MAE. Two remedies are worth testing: a
floor or clip on the reconstructed correction, or a two-stage gate that decides
zero against non-zero before regressing magnitude at all. [GAP: the direction of
this effect has held across every version of the comparison so far, but the
segment magnitudes in `3.4` are pending regeneration, since the FNN predictions
there are stale. Do not quote segment skill figures until `3.3` and `3.4` have
been re-run.]

One design shortcut needs its own note, because it looks like a limitation and
probably is not. Hyperparameters are searched only within the kernel that won the
scan, rather than running a full grid inside every kernel. An independent
full per-kernel search exists in `models_predictions/SVR/residual_kernelgrid/` and
was previously read as confirming the shortcut. It can no longer be read that way.
Those artifacts date from before the zero-mile-trip drop, and the giveaway is the
baseline rather than the models: at h3_7/daily the full-grid run records a baseline
validation MAE of 14.658 against 15.830 in the current run, and the historical mean
is a property of the data alone, not of the search. The two runs are therefore
scored on different datasets, and on the current artifacts only two of six levels
even select the same kernel and feature set. [GAP: re-run the full per-kernel grid
search on the post-drop data, or drop the claim that the two-stage shortcut is
validated. As it stands the check is untested against the data actually reported
here. Note also that the `level_comparison.csv` this comparison is usually cited
from does not exist under `residual_kernelgrid/`; only the per-level bundles do.]

Three improvement levers remain that do not reintroduce autoregressive signal.
Weather enters the model as a single citywide hourly series, so it varies across
hours but never across cells within an hour, which leaves both weather-by-hour and
weather-by-location interactions unexplored, and makes finer or spatially resolved
weather data worth acquiring. POI enters as counts per cell, where a distance to
the nearest POI of each category would carry more information about why a cell
generates trips. The permutation and drop-block analysis supports that ordering:
after `base_demand`, the daily levels depend most on the POI block (+5.5% MAE at
h3_7/daily, +9.4% at census/daily, +13.2% at community/daily when it is removed),
while the hourly levels depend on history instead (+148%, +32% and +22%
respectively). [GAP: those figures are the direct SVR's permutation run in `3.2a`;
`3.2b`'s residual-specific ablation was not regenerated this run and is currently
unverified against the post-drop data.]

We frame the taxi driver's home charging as a Markov Decision Process and solve it
with Q-learning. The agent sets the charging power in 15-minute steps between the
2 p.m. arrival and 4 p.m. departure, trading off recharging cost against the risk
of not meeting the (stochastic) energy demand for the working day.
